header.title: Comparing Sampling Methods
header.subtitle: Matching the method to the population and the question

meta.ac9-descriptor-text: AC9M8ST02 — analyse and report on the distribution of data from primary and secondary sources using random and non-random sampling techniques to select and study samples. AC9M8ST01 — investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, experiment and observation, and explain the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through these techniques.
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: A representative sample depends on the nature of the population and the question being considered
meta.lesson-focus: Compare simple random, systematic, stratified, quota, cluster, convenience and judgement sampling; match the method to the population structure; define probabilistic terms — random, sample space, sample, sample distribution.

html.section0_intro: Last lesson you learned that a large sample can still be biased — size never fixes who was left out. Today we compare the actual methods used to choose a sample. These three questions check the ideas of census, sample and bias that we build on. (Referenced against the SA Curriculum, Mathematics R–10 Prototype 2.)
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's statistics.

In 1936 an American magazine, the Literary Digest, mailed out a survey and collected a staggering 2.4 million replies predicting who would win the presidential election.

A young pollster named George Gallup used a carefully chosen sample of only about 50,000 people.

Gallup was right. The 2.4-million survey was badly wrong.

The magazine drew its names from car and telephone owners — wealthier people, not a fair slice of all voters. A huge sample chosen the wrong way lost to a small sample chosen the right way. The method of sampling matters more than the size. Today we meet seven sampling methods, split them into random and non-random, and learn to match each one to the population and the question it suits.
html.vocab_cards:
Sample
Tap to flip
A selected part of the population, chosen to stand in for the whole.
60 students chosen from a school of 900.
Random
Tap to flip
Every member has a known, non-zero chance of selection, and no individual choice can be predicted in advance.
Names drawn from a hat — not "whoever is nearest".
Sample space
Tap to flip
The set of all possible outcomes that could be selected — everyone the method could reach.
For a class draw, the sample space is all 30 names in the hat.
Sample distribution
Tap to flip
How the values in the sample are spread — the shape you get when you graph the sampled data.
The spread of heights among the 30 students you measured.
Representative sample
Tap to flip
A sample whose make-up mirrors the population, so its distribution roughly matches the whole. Whether a sample is representative depends on the population and the question.
A stratified sample that keeps each year level in proportion.
html.sort_activity:
Sort each sampling method
Simple random (names from a hat) Systematic (every 10th on a list) Stratified (random pick within each group) Cluster (survey all of randomly chosen groups) Quota (fill group totals by convenience) Convenience (whoever is easiest to reach) Judgement (an expert hand-picks)

🎲 Random (probability) sampling

✋ Non-random sampling

💡 A method is random only if every member has a known chance of being picked. In quota, convenience and judgement sampling a person chooses who gets in — so chances are neither known nor equal.
html.worked_example:
A sports club has 20 members in three squads: Juniors (10), Intermediates (6) and Seniors (4). The committee wants a representative sample of 10 members to trial new training times. Use stratified sampling.

1
Identify the strata and the sampling fraction
Split the population into its natural groups (strata), then find what fraction of the whole population we are sampling.
Strata: Juniors 10, Intermediates 6, Seniors 4  →  total = 20
Sampling fraction = samplepopulation = 1020 = 12
2
Apply the fraction to each stratum
Take 12 of each squad, then choose those members at random within the squad.
Juniors: 12 × 10 = 5  ·  Intermediates: 12 × 6 = 3  ·  Seniors: 12 × 4 = 2
3
Verify the total and explain why stratified fits
Check the parts add to the sample, and connect the method to the population and the question.
5 + 3 + 2 = 10 ✓   and every squad appears in proportion to its size.
Why stratified The squads differ in size and may want different training times, so each must be represented in proportion — the method is chosen to match the population's structure and the question being asked.

retrieval.q: A census collects data from every member of the population. What is a sample? (A) every member of the population (B) a selected part of the population (C) only the largest group
retrieval.hint: It's a subset chosen to stand in for the whole population.

retrieval.q: True or false: making a biased sample much bigger removes the bias. Type true or false.
retrieval.hint: A large but poorly chosen sample is still biased — size can't fix who was left out.

retrieval.q: A sample is only useful if it truly ______ the population it comes from. (A) copies it exactly (B) represents it (C) outnumbers it
retrieval.hint: We want the sample to mirror the whole population - a smaller version with the same mix.

matchTerms.html: Population splits into subgroups of different sizes that must appear in proportion
Population spread across many natural groups; reaching individuals is too costly
Members already sit in a fixed order or list (a production line)
Small, uniform population with a complete list; everyone equally likely
Subgroup totals must be filled fast, with no random step

weDo.q: The population is all students across six year levels of different sizes. Which method makes sure each year level appears in the right proportion? (A) convenience (B) stratified (C) judgement
weDo.hint: We need every subgroup represented in proportion to its size.

weDo.q: Why would surveying only the Year 12 common room be a poor choice? (A) it's a convenience sample that leaves out five year levels (B) it's stratified (C) it's too random
weDo.hint: Think about who gets left out.

weDo.q: True or false: doubling a Year-12-only survey would make it represent the whole school. Type true or false.
weDo.hint: More of one year level still ignores the other five — a bigger biased sample is still biased.

checkpoint.q:
Quick check. A shop asks the first 15 customers after opening about its opening hours. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is a convenience sample.
(B) Early customers may not represent evening shoppers.
(C) The first 15 customers form a random sample.
checkpoint.hint: Whoever happens to be first is convenience, not a random draw — chances are not equal.

checkpoint.q:
Quick check. Stratified and quota sampling both split the population into groups. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Stratified sampling selects randomly within each group.
(B) Quota sampling fills each group's total by convenience.
(C) The two methods are identical.
checkpoint.hint: The random step inside each group is what separates stratified from quota.

practice1.q:
Scenario: A student surveys the first 20 people they meet in the canteen queue. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is a convenience sample — the easiest people to reach.
(B) Because no names were written down first, it counts as a random sample.
(C) Canteen-queue students might not represent people who bring lunch from home.
practice1.hint: In a random sample every member has a known, equal chance. Grabbing whoever is nearest gives no such chance.

fb.A: A is true — reaching for whoever is easiest is exactly what a convenience sample is.
fb.C: C is true — that possible bias is the risk of convenience sampling.

practice1.q:
Scenario: An online poll on a football club's fan page asks 10,000 fans whether the club is the best in the league. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Only people who already like the club tend to visit the page, so the sample is biased.
(B) Collecting 10,000 responses instead of 1,000 removes the bias.
(C) A smaller random sample of all league supporters would be more trustworthy.
practice1.hint: Bias is about WHO is in the sample, not how many. A bigger biased sample is still biased.

fb.B: B is the lie: 10,000 self-selected fans are still a one-sided crowd — size can't fix it.
fb.A: A is true — the fan page draws a self-selected, one-sided crowd.

practice1.q:
Scenario: A researcher splits a school into year levels, then randomly selects students from each year in proportion to its size. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is stratified sampling.
(B) Selection within each year level is random.
(C) This is exactly the same as quota sampling.
practice1.hint: Stratified uses RANDOM selection inside each group; quota fills the totals by convenience, with no random step.

fb.C: C is the lie: the random step inside each stratum makes it stratified, not quota.
fb.A: A is true — dividing into strata then sampling each in proportion is stratified sampling.

practice1.q:
Scenario: Every student's name is put in a hat and 30 are drawn out. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is simple random sampling.
(B) Every student has an equal chance of being chosen.
(C) Students who sit at the front are more likely to be drawn.
practice1.hint: In a fair draw from a hat, where you sit has no effect on your chance of selection.

practice1.q:
Scenario: A factory checks every 50th tin coming off the production line. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is systematic sampling.
(B) The gap between chosen items is fixed at 50.
(C) The inspector personally picks the tins that look faulty.
practice1.hint: Systematic sampling follows a fixed interval; choosing by appearance would be judgement sampling.

practice1.q:
Scenario: A council divides a city into suburbs, randomly picks 4 suburbs, and surveys everyone living in them. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is cluster sampling.
(B) Whole groups (suburbs) are selected, then everyone inside is surveyed.
(C) This guarantees every suburb in the city is represented.
practice1.hint: Cluster sampling surveys only the chosen suburbs — the ones left out are not represented.

practice1.q:
Scenario: An expert hand-picks the 12 students she believes best represent the school. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is judgement sampling.
(B) The choice relies on the expert's opinion.
(C) Personal opinion cannot introduce bias into the sample.
practice1.hint: Any choice based on opinion can carry that person's bias — the main weakness of judgement sampling.

practice1.q:
Scenario: An interviewer is told to survey 20 teenagers and 20 adults, choosing whoever is willing to stop and talk. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is quota sampling.
(B) The subgroup totals (20 and 20) are set in advance.
(C) Each person had an equal, random chance of being selected.
practice1.hint: Quota sampling fills the totals by convenience — no random step, so chances are not equal.

fb.C: C is the lie: quota sampling has NO random step, so it is not the same as stratified sampling.

practice1.q:
Scenario: A blogger surveys only their own followers because it is quick and free. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is a convenience sample.
(B) It is convenient but may not represent the wider population.
(C) Being easy to collect makes the data more accurate.
practice1.hint: Ease of collection says nothing about accuracy — convenient samples are often the least representative.

practice1.q:
Scenario: We call a selection method random. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Random means every outcome in the sample space has a known chance of occurring.
(B) In a random sample, no individual's selection can be predicted in advance.
(C) 'Random' just means 'whatever is most convenient at the time'.
practice1.hint: Random has a precise meaning: known, non-zero chances for each member — not 'whatever is easiest'.

fb.C: C is the lie — confusing 'random' with 'convenient' is the classic error.

practice2.q:
Scenario: Two studies both aim for 60% girls, 40% boys. Study P randomly selects names within each group; Study Q lets interviewers approach anyone until each total is filled. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Study P is stratified sampling.
(B) Study Q is quota sampling.
(C) Because both end with the same 60:40 split, both are stratified samples.
practice2.hint: The final proportions can match, but only the study with a random step inside each group is stratified.

fb.C: C is the lie: matching proportions doesn't make Q stratified — it lacks the random selection that defines stratified sampling.

practice2.q:
Scenario: A survey left off everyone without internet access, then doubled its sample size to improve results. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Doubling the size does not reach the people who were excluded.
(B) The larger sample is now representative of the whole population.
(C) The bias comes from who is missing, not from the sample being too small.
practice2.hint: If a whole group is excluded, adding more of the included group cannot fix it — size never repairs coverage.

fb.B: B is the lie: a bigger sample from the same biased source stays biased.

practice2.q:
Scenario: A teacher grabs whichever exercise books are on top of the pile to check homework. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Books on top were probably handed in last, so they are a particular group.
(B) This is a convenience sample.
(C) Grabbing the top books gives every book an equal chance, so it is random.
practice2.hint: Position in the pile is not random — late finishers cluster on top, so chances are not equal.

fb.C: C is the lie: 'easy to grab' is convenience, not random selection.

practice2.q:
Scenario: A researcher randomly chooses 3 of the school's 30 classes and surveys every student in those 3 classes. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is cluster sampling.
(B) Students in the 27 unchosen classes have no chance of being in the sample.
(C) This is stratified sampling because the school was split into classes.
practice2.hint: Stratified samples take some members from EVERY group; cluster sampling surveys only the groups that were picked.

fb.C: C is the lie: sampling only the chosen groups is cluster, not stratified.

practice2.q:
Scenario: Every 10th house on a street is surveyed, but the larger corner houses happen to fall on every 10th position. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) The method is systematic sampling.
(B) A hidden pattern in the list can make a systematic sample unrepresentative.
(C) A fixed interval always guarantees a representative sample.
practice2.hint: If the list has a repeating pattern that lines up with the interval, systematic sampling can go badly wrong.

practice2.q:
Scenario: A principal picks the students she thinks are 'typical' to represent the school's opinion. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is judgement sampling.
(B) Whether the sample is representative depends on the population and the question being asked.
(C) Because an expert chose them, the sample is guaranteed to be representative.
practice2.hint: Expert choice still carries opinion and bias; representativeness depends on the population and question, not on who picked.

practice3.q:
Scenario: A national study needs opinions from a population spread across 500 remote towns, with three age bands that must appear in the right proportions, on a tight travel budget. A statistician randomly selects 8 towns, then within each randomly samples people to hit the age-band proportions. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Choosing 8 towns at random is a cluster step, chosen partly to cut travel cost.
(B) Sampling to fixed age proportions within each town uses a stratified idea.
(C) This design is pure convenience sampling with no random element.
practice3.hint: There are two random steps (towns, then people) — the opposite of convenience sampling.

fb.C: C is the lie: the design is a random, multi-stage method, not convenience sampling.

practice3.q:
Scenario: Poll X asks 200 randomly chosen voters; Poll Y asks 50,000 people who chose to phone in. Poll Y predicts the wrong election result. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Poll Y's phone-in method is self-selecting and biased.
(B) Poll Y's huge size makes it more reliable than Poll X.
(C) Poll X's smaller random sample can beat Poll Y's larger biased one.
practice3.hint: The classic result: a small random sample outperforms a giant self-selected one. Size cannot cure bias.

fb.B: B is the lie: 50,000 self-selected responses are still biased — Poll X's random 200 is more trustworthy.

practice3.q:
Scenario: A market team must reflect a city that is 70% adults, 30% teens. Team A draws names randomly from a full register until the split is reached; Team B sends staff to a mall to approach people until 70 adults and 30 teens agree. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) Team A is stratified; Team B is quota.
(B) Team B's mall location may exclude people who never visit malls.
(C) Team A and Team B use identical methods because their proportions match.
practice3.hint: Same proportions, different methods: only Team A selects randomly within each group. Quota (B) has no random step.

fb.C: C is the lie: matching the 70:30 split doesn't make quota the same as stratified — the random step is missing.

practice3.q:
Scenario: Researchers record the heights of a sample and draw the sample distribution to compare with the population. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) A sample distribution shows how the sampled values are spread.
(B) A representative sample's distribution should roughly mirror the population's.
(C) A convenience sample always produces a distribution identical to the population's.
practice3.hint: Convenience samples often produce a skewed distribution — there is no guarantee it matches the population.

fb.C: C is the lie: convenience samples frequently give a distribution that does NOT match the population.

exitProbs.q:
Scenario: A café asks only its lunchtime regulars to rate a new menu. Which claim is the LIE?
(A) This is a convenience sample.
(B) Lunchtime regulars may not represent breakfast or dinner customers.
(C) Because it was easy and quick, it is a random sample.
exitProbs.hint: Easy and quick describes convenience, not random selection.

exitProbs.q: Name the method: a population is split into year levels and students are chosen at random from each year in proportion to its size. Type one word.
exitProbs.hint: Random selection inside each proportional group — not quota, which has no random step.

exitProbs.q: In your own words, explain the difference between stratified and quota sampling, and why a bigger sample does not fix a biased method.
exitProbs.hint: Mention the random step that stratified has and quota lacks, and that bias is about WHO is left out — not size.
